references.title_full: The Effect of Cooperative and Mastery Learning Methods on Primary Grade Students' Learning and Retention of Economic Concepts
references.authors: Laney James D; Frerichs Dean K; Frerichs Linda P; Pat Luke K;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Empirical studies have shown the positive effects of combining cooperative and mastery learning methods on mathematics achievement higher order questioning skills, and originality, but little is known, at present, about the effects of cooperative-mastery learning in other subject areas or on other cognitive outcomes. The problem of this study was to explore the effects of cooperative and mastery learning methods, alone and in combination, on first and second grade students' learning and retention of basic economic concepts. A 2 X 2 (cooperative X mastery) factorial design compared the achievement of one hundred-twenty students who were individually randomly assigned (using grade level as a stratification variable) to one of four treatment conditions?instruction on basic economic concepts using (1) cooperative learning, (2) mastery learning, (3) cooperative-mastery learning, or (4) a control treatment (no cooperative or mastery learning). All subjects were administered a written pretest, post-test, and delayed post-test on their understanding of economic concepts. To further probe children's understanding of economic concepts, a randomly selected sub-sample of sixty- four students was interviewed using an oral pretest, post-test, and delayed post-test. Overall, the results support the superiority of the cooperative-mastery learning method over either method alone in promoting the acquisition and retention of economic concepts. Pretest data verified the initial equivalence of groups. The cooperative-mastery learning group outperformed (a) the control group on all post-tests and delayed post-tests and (b) the cooperative learning group on all post-tests and delayed post-tests except the written post-test. By delayed post-test on the oral measure, the cooperative-mastery learning group was also outperforming the mastery learning group. As further evidence of the superiority of the cooperative-mastery learning method, the mean score of the cooperative-mastery learning group was greater than the combined mean scores of the mastery and cooperative learning groups on the oral post-test and delayed post-test. The authors suggest that the cooperative-mastery learning method is in line with current early childhood practices and has the capacity for simultaneously boosting the conceptual development and language development of young children. This capacity is said to stem from the method's provision of (a) specific, positive feedback, (b) a social context for sustained effort and involvement in a topic, (c) child?child communication exchanges, and (d) adult?child communication exchanges.

references.title_full: The short-term impact of two classroom-based preventive interventions on aggressive and shy behaviors and poor achievement
references.authors: Dolan L J  Kellam S G  Brown C H  Werthamer-Larsson L   Rebok G W  Mayer L S  Laudolff J   Turkkan J S  Ford C   Wheeler L
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Two classroom-based preventive interventions were carried out on an epidemiologically defined, varied population of children in a metropolitan area in the United States. This is a report of the short-term impact and specificity of the two interventions from fall through spring of first grade. The first intervention, the Good Behavior Game, was aimed at reducing aggressive behavior and shy behavior. Aggressive behavior has been shown to be an important developmental antecedent in first grade of later delinquency and heavy drug use, particularly when coupled with shy behavior. The second intervention, Mastery Learning, was designed to improve poor reading achievement, which has been shown to be an antecedent for later depressive symptoms, as well as a correlate of aggressive and shy behaviors. Each of the two interventions had a significant and very specific impact only on its own proximal target(s). In addition to main effects, there were theoretically important variations of impacts among subgroups of children. The Good Behavior Game appeared to have a greater impact in reducing aggressive behavior among the more aggressive children. The nature of the impact of Mastery Learning differed by gender, with female high achievers benefiting more from the intervention than female low achievers, and male low achievers benefiting more than male high achievers. Developmental epidemiologically based preventive trials provide a powerful means of addressing questions about etiology and development, particularly around the issue of the malleability of developmental processes. Important questions that future work could test are whether achievement is improved by improving aggressive or shy behaviors and whether aggressive or shy behaviors are improved by improving achievement. Such investigation would inform our understanding of their etiology. © 1993.

references.title_full: Three types of programmed learning and the conventional teaching of the nuclear chemistry portion of a high school chemistry course.
references.authors: Darnowski Vincent S;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The problem investigated in the study was a comparison of the learning and retention of the facts and principles of nuclear chemistry in the high school chemistry course using three forms of programed materials and the conventional lecture-demonstration method of teaching. The three forms of programed materials were linear short-step, long-step linear, and branched programs. A list of operational objectives and an outline of content objectives both were prepared prior to the preparation of the short-step program. The program was drafted and initially tested with a full high school chemistry class. In further development and revision, segments of the program were presented to several high school students and two experienced high school teachers. A final testing of the program was accomplished by using it with a full high school class. The branched form of the program was prepared from the basic form by identifying key items and rearranging the basic program to allow students who answered the key items correctly to skip over practice and review frames. The longstep form of the program was prepared by deleting repeating, practice and review frames. A multiple choice, forty-four item achievement test in nuclear chemistry was constructed. Preliminary evaluations in three high schools with intact classes were each followed by a revision to produce a more reliable instrument. The basic test was used as both pre-test and retention test for / 2 the study. The post-test was an alternative form of the basic test. Validation of the test instrument and the programs was carried on by submitting them to a jury of five experienced high school teachers. Students who participated in the four study treatments were from two high schools in the same school district. The approximately 150 students initially in each group were reduced to twenty-six students per group when matched across groups on total number of science courses and total number of mathematics courses taken, measured intelligence and reading scores. During the study, experimental programs were administered by the usual classroom teachers of chemistry. The time for classroom consideration of nuclear chemistry was seven class days. The pre-test was administered immediately before the study of nuclear chemistry was initiated. The post-test was given the class period following completion of the study of nuclear chemistry and the retention test was given two months after the study was completed. All groups learned a significant amount during their study of nuclear chemistry. Statistical comparison of pretest post-test gain using an analysis of covariance showed that the groups using programs, considered as a unit, gained significantly more than the control group. Between groups comparisons using a t-test on gain means showed that only the pre-test post-test gain by the group using the branched form of the program was significantly greater than the gain 3 of the control group. On the post-test of achievement, the variance of the group using the branched form of the program was significantly smaller than that of the control group. The correlation of measured intelligence and achievement was significantly smaller for the group using the long-step program than the control group. Statistical comparison of retention test scores using an analysis of covariance showed that the control group had a significantly greater retention of the facts and principles of nuclear chemistry when compared to all groups using programed materials. The following conclusions could be made regarding the study  1. Students using a branched form of a program to study nuclear chemistry achieved significantly more than those using the conventional lecture-demonstration method. Students using a long-step form of the program learned more than the control but the difference in gain means was not significant. 2. Students studying nuclear chemistry using the conventional lecture-demonstration method retained significantly more than those using the three forms of programed materials. 3. Individual differences were cared for at least in part as students using the branched form of the program had a smaller variance on the final test of achievement than those in the control group. Also, the correlation between achievement and measured intelligence was significantly smaller for the group using the long-step program than for the control.

references.title_full: The short-term impact of two classroom-based preventive interventions on aggressive and shy behaviors and poor achievement
references.authors: Dolan L J  Kellam S G  Brown C H  Werthamer-Larsson L   Rebok G W  Mayer L S  Laudolff J   Turkkan J S  Ford C   Wheeler L
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Two classroom-based preventive interventions were carried out on an epidemiologically defined, varied population of children in a metropolitan area in the United States. This is a report of the short-term impact and specificity of the two interventions from fall through spring of first grade. The first intervention, the Good Behavior Game, was aimed at reducing aggressive behavior and shy behavior. Aggressive behavior has been shown to be an important developmental antecedent in first grade of later delinquency and heavy drug use, particularly when coupled with shy behavior. The second intervention, Mastery Learning, was designed to improve poor reading achievement, which has been shown to be an antecedent for later depressive symptoms, as well as a correlate of aggressive and shy behaviors. Each of the two interventions had a significant and very specific impact only on its own proximal target(s). In addition to main effects, there were theoretically important variations of impacts among subgroups of children. The Good Behavior Game appeared to have a greater impact in reducing aggressive behavior among the more aggressive children. The nature of the impact of Mastery Learning differed by gender, with female high achievers benefiting more from the intervention than female low achievers, and male low achievers benefiting more than male high achievers. Developmental epidemiologically based preventive trials provide a powerful means of addressing questions about etiology and development, particularly around the issue of the malleability of developmental processes. Important questions that future work could test are whether achievement is improved by improving aggressive or shy behaviors and whether aggressive or shy behaviors are improved by improving achievement. Such investigation would inform our understanding of their etiology. © 1993.

references.title_full: The Effects of Cooperative Mastery Learning Strategies on Mathematics Achievement
references.authors: Mevarech Zemira R;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This study investigated the effects of student-teams using mastery learning strategies (STML) on mathematics achievement of fifth-grade children (N = 134). The experiment used a 2 x 2 (Student Teams x Mastery Learning) factorial design. Results showed higher achievement gains for pupils exposed to STML than for those exposed through more traditional instruction. The data further indicated that learning in small groups promoted only computational skills whereas mastery learning strategies improved both computation and comprehension. In addition, the benefits of the methods for high-, medium-, and low-ability students were examined and discussed.

references.title_full: Mastery Learning and Academic Achievement
references.authors: Miles Kent S;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: During the 2006-2007 school year, 14% of the eighth-grade mathematics students at the study campus failed to meet advancement criteria on the Georgia Criterion Referenced Competency Test (CRCT). The purpose of this quantitative pretest-posttest and control-group design study was to first investigate the effects of a mastery goal approach to instruction on eighth-grade mathematic students’ academic ability, and also to examine the effects of the treatment on motivational constructs. For the first portion of the study, two groups of students, 43 in the control group and 36 in the treatment group, were examined to determine the effect of the treatment on the participants’ academic achievement on the STAR Math assessment. An independent-measures t test was used to evaluate the mean difference (MD ) in the scaled scores gains from STAR Math assessments to determine academic achievement, which indicated the treatment group had significantly higher achievement gains than the control group, MD = 32.44, p < .001, and d = .53. Next, a repeated-measures study of 57 students used a Motivational Orientation Inventory (MOI) as a pretest and posttest to determine any changes, as a result of the treatment, on the students’ academic motivational orientation, perceptions of classroom goal structures, and academic efficacy. Paired-samples t tests were conducted on the mean of each motivational construct in the MOI with the results indicating significant changes in the students’ performance-avoidance goal orientation. Findings can be used to enhance positive social change by providing mastery learning structures including individualized student pacing of instruction, remediation and retesting of standards, and student assessment based on mastery of material in order to motivate students to learn and promote higher levels of academic achievement.

references.title_full: A comparison of mastery learning feedback systems, affecting achievement in chemistry
references.title_parent: The Annual Meeting of the American Educational Research Association (ERIC Document Rekoduction Service No. ED 139 650)
references.authors: Swanson D H;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The effectiveness of a Keller and Bloom mastery learning program for high school science students was examined by comparing remediation strategies of both programs and that of a traditional strategy. The data gathered in the experiment in chemistry were from a pre- and post-achievement test. Cognitive achievement was statistically different (p < .025). Additional analysis revealed the greatest difference was between a Bloom and a traditional strategy. Gain score analyses failed to produce any significant differences. A Chi-square analysis of the number of objectives achieved produced significant values of .004 and .034, respectively, for the Keller and Bloom groups over the traditional group.

references.title_full: The Effect of Flexible Modular Scheduling on Student Achievement in BSCS Biology.
references.authors: Moore Billy Fulton;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Reported is a study to compare the achievement of selected 10th-grade biology students on a traditional schedule with selected 10th-grade biology students on a flexible modular schedule. Both groups studied the blue version of the Biological Sciences Curriculum Study (BSCS) materials. Students were paired in the groups on the basis of their scores on Test 2, Background in Natural Sciences, and the composite of the Iowa Tests of Educational Development. Achievement was measured by use of the BSCS Comprehensive Final Examination for first year biology students. Additional data came from scores on the Brown-Holtzman Survey of Study Habits. Twenty-nine matched pairs of students were involved in the final data analysis. No significant differences were found in achievement  in study habits, study attitudes, and study orientation  nor did school organizational type affect student achievement in BSCS biology. (Author/PEB)

references.title_full: Diagnosis, Remediation, and Locus of Control
references.authors: Saunders-Harris Ramona ; Yeany Russell H;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The influence of locus of control, diagnosis, and remediation on immediate and retained achievement and attitudes of middle school science students was the focus of this study. Subjects in the experiment were assessed for locus of control and experienced one of three treatments  no diagnosis or remediation  diagnosis with no remediation  or, diagnosis and remediation. Immediate achievement was measured at two points during the experiment, and retention was measured 30 days following the experiment. Diagnosis and remediation proved to be significantly effective in increasing retained achievement. Internal locus of control subjects out-scored external subjects in the areas of both immediate and retained achievement. Whites achieved higher than blacks in retention. Attitudes of all groups tended to be positive. These findings suggest that diagnostic or diagnostic and remedial instruction is an effective means of increasing the retention level of middle school students.

references.title_full: Altering Teacher and Pupil Behavior with Mastery Teaching
references.authors: Okey James R;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This study's main purpose was to determine the effects a mastery teaching strategy would have on pupil achievement. A total of 21 teachers participated  results are reported for the subgroup of third and fourth grade teachers (n=5). Achievement of pupils favored the mastery group for each of the teachers. (DT)

references.title_full: Mastery versus nonmastery instruction with varying test item feedback treatments
references.authors: Wentling Tim L;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Used a 3 * 2 * 2 factorial design with factors of feedback specificity (total, partial, or none), instructional strategy (mastery or nonmastery), and mental ability (high and low scores on Otis-Lennon Mental Ability Test). 116 male high school students were Ss for the 5-wk study. The mastery strategy was superior in terms of immediate and delayed achievement, but Ss required 50% more time to complete instructions with no difference in attitude. Partial item feedback for unit tests was superior on both immediate achievement and attitude with no difference in retention. A mastery strategy with partial item feedback appears most desirable when time trade-off is justifiable. (26 ref.) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2010 APA, all rights reserved).

references.title_full: Improving Reading Comprehension: Embedding Diverse Learning Strategies within a Mastery Learning Instructional Framework.
references.title_parent: Paper presented at the annual meeting of the American Educational Research Association, San Francisco. (ERIC Document Reproduction Service No. ED 170 698)
references.authors: Jones Beau F; Monsaas J A; Katims M ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The paper describes the theoretical background, implementation and preliminary results of the Chicago Mastery Learning/Learning Strategies reading program for upper elementary school students. Reading research and learning strategies research are pulled together to support the argument that the teaching of diverse learning strategies can improve reading comprehension and that the strategies should be embedded within the mastery learning framework. Since the purpose of this study was to develop and field test the materials, a controlled experiment was not conducted. Field test results (involving six classrooms matched on four variables related to achievement) strongly suggested that teaching learning strategies improves reading comprehension. (Author)

references.title_full: Development and evaluation of an individualized learning unit in science for the junior high school
references.authors: Peterson Richard Smith;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This study involved the development of a conceptually oriented curriculum framework in science for grades seven through nine, the individualization of one learning unit selected from the framework, and the design of an investigation to analyze change in the acquisition of subject matter content between students in individualized and in lecture/demonstration-centered patterns of instruction. The subject matter content consisted of scientific facts and principles embraced by the concept Matter Is Particulate. Fifty-eight classes were selected from six junior high schools in the Jordan and Weber School Districts to participate in the study. Class enrollment ranged from 16 students in one class to 41 in another. Of the 58 classes selected, 31 were taught by individualized patterns of instruction with a mastery learning orientation  the remaining 27 classes were taught by lecture/demonstration-centered patterns of instruction. The 58 classes were taught by 23 different teachers. During the Fall of 1969, the students participated in a pretesting program which included a subject matter achievement test and a mental maturity (l.Q.) test. The post-testing program, conducted nine to twelve weeks later, involved the administration of an alternate form of the same achievement test to determine student gains in subject matter content. The curriculum framework, which included an outline of the major scientific principles embraced by the concept Matter Is Particulate, was given to each teacher in both the individualized and the lecture/demonstration-centered patterns of instruction. The subject matter outline was Identical for both groups. Data used in this study were obtained from three tests whose validity and reliability were well established  Interaction of Matter and Energy Experimental Achievement Test Interaction of Matter and Energy Achievement Test, and the Verbal Reasoning and Numerical Abilities sections of the Differential Aptitude Tests battery. The following conclusions were drawn from the data analyzed in this investigation. 1. There was a relationship, significant at the .001 level, between the acquisition of subject matter content and the method of instruction. Students in individualized classes earned higher gain scores on the achievement test than those in lecture/demonstration-centered classes. 2. There was a significant relationship at the .001 level between the acquisition of subject matter content and the I.Q. level of the student. Students with high mental ability made higher gain scores than those with lower mental ability. 3. There was no significant relationship between the subject matter content and the following factors  (a) sex  (b) method and sex  (c) method and I.Q. level  and (d) method, I.Q. level, and sex. 4. There was a significant relationship at the .01 level between the subject matter content and a combination of I.Q. level and sex.

references.title_full: An evaluation study of teaching seventh grade mathematics incorporating team teaching, individualized instruction, and team supervision utilizing the strategy of learning for mastery
references.authors: Beul B T;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This study was conducted at a suburban school district in west St. Louis County, Missouri. The investigation was executed at two of the five junior high schools in the school district with an approximate enrollment of 1,050 students at each of the two schools and approximately 350 students in seventh-grade classes at each of the two schools. The investigation consisted of 202 students in the experimental group and 199 students in a control group who were randomly assigned to seventh-grade mathematics classes by way of a computer. Teachers and students in the  control group were in a self-contained classroom using some form of a "traditional" approach. The students in the experimental group were learning under a team-teaching, individualized-instruction approach utilizing the strategy of learning for mastery. All students involved in the experimental and control group took the SRA Achievement Test and the Mathematics Attitude-Interest Test as the pre-tests for this investigation.  At the end of the investigation, all participants took the SRA Achievement Test and the Mathematics Attitude-Interest Test again as post-tests.  T-tests for the significance of means were used for analyzing the data.  Students achieved significantly more mathematics in the team-teaching individualized instruction program utilizing the strategy of learning for mastery than students in the traditional classroom program. It also can be concluded, that according to the attitude test given, students of the team teaching individualized instruction program did not improve in attitude or interest in mathematics and neither did the students in the traditional classroom program.

references.title_full: A study of mastery learning and its effects on achievement of sixth grade social studies students
references.authors: Wyckoff D B;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purpose of this study was to compare the effects on achievement of using a mastery learning strategy for teaching selected anthropological concepts to sixth grade social studies students with the effects of using a more conventional classroom teaching strategy for teaching selected anthropological concepts to sixth grade social studies students. Methods and Procedure  two intact classes of 26 children each used the teach-test-reteach-retest feedback/correction process (mastery learning strategy) while two other intact classes of 27 and 28 each were taught by conventional methods which did not utilize the mastery learning strategy. Materials developed by The Anthropology Curriculum Project, University of Georgia, 1972, were used by the children and teachers involved in the study.  A 70% median score was required in each experimental group before the total group could progress to the next selected anthropological concept. Peer tutoring was primarily used for the reteaching section of the teach-test-reteach-retest (mastery learning) strategy of teaching. The hypotheses were examined by analysis of variance considering treatment by sex, by IQ, and by reading level with the anthropology achievement test score as the dependent variable. Use of the two-way factorial design allowed for testing of interaction between independent variables. The .05 level of significance was used to,accept or reject the various hypotheses. Results  the experimental method of teaching produced superior effects with male students. The mastery learning strategy of teaching had a decidedly positive effect upon low reading level students and upon low IQ students. The experimental method of teaching had no differential effect upon high reading level students, upon high IQ students, or upon female students. Conclusions  no significant differences at the .05 level were obtained on the overall comparison between mean achievement scores from those students receiving mastery learning treatment and from the students who did not receive mastery learning treatment.

references.title_full: Effects of a four-year Follow Through program on economically disadvantaged children
references.authors: Abelson Willa D; Zigler Edward ; DeBlasi Cheryl L;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Longitudinal and cross-sectional comparisons were made of 109 economically disadvantaged children in 1 Follow-Through and several non-Follow-Through primary school programs. A longitudinal comparison was also made of the economically disadvantaged and nondisadvantaged children in the Follow-Through program. Clear-cut program effects were found in the 4th yr (grade 3) when Follow-Through children were superior to non-Follow-Through children on IQ, achievement, and social-motivational measures. The Follow-Through program did not result in the economically disadvantaged children attaining the level of intellectual achievement displayed by the nondisadvantaged children. (30 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)

references.title_full: Effects of selected mastery learning strategies in terms of articulation problems in French 3 classes at Bellevue High School.
references.authors: McKim Lester Wayne;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This study was conducted to determine whether selected mastery learning strategies might serve as a partial solution to articulation problems in level 3 French. The central question posited was one of determining whether certain desired learning outcomes (and those logically related to smooth program articulation) were encouraged by the utilization of selected mastery learning strategies. Specifically, the investigation was directed to two related questions  1) Can mastery learning strategies lead to achievement gains? and 2) Can these strategies at the same time produce a lesser variance in student achievement? Two null hypotheses related to the amount of learning and one null hypothesis related to the variability of posttest scores were developed. The selected mastery learning strategies used in the study were additional information about the content and expectations of each unit of work before the work was begun, frequent testing and detailed feedback on the results of the tests, and extra attempts to improve performance on tests. The researcher also considered the practicality of applying mastery learning strategies to secondary school instruction in terms of time constraints of a traditionally scheduled school, required alterations in the curriculum, amount of teacher time required for planning and evaluation, and identification of strategies critical to success. Seventy-four students taking level 3 French comprised the research sample. The MLA-Cooperative Foreign Language Tests were administered at the beginning of the study and students were randomly assigned on a matchedpair basis to a control or an experimental group on the basis of measures of competence in listening, speaking, reading, and writing. After ten weeks of instruction, parallel forms of the standardized test were administered to measure gains made during the research period and to determine the variability of students' competencies as indicated by posttest scores. Statistical analyses of the data (t-tests and analyses of variance) indicated that 1) subjects in both groups made significant gains in listening, speaking, and writing, but not in reading  2) that subjects were not significantly different with regard to the mean gain scores  3) that from analysis of the subsections of the tests, both groups were basically the same (the experimental group made significant gains on 14 of the subsections while the control group made significant gains on 13 subsections)  and 4) that there was no significant difference between the variability of the posttest scores for the two groups.

references.title_full: An Investigation into the Effects of a Modified Mastery Strategy on Achievement in a High School Human Physiology Unit.
references.title_parent: Journal of Research in Science Teaching

references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Determined if modifying Bloom's mastery strategy improves science achievement during a six week human physiology unit. Findings indicate only a small degree of improvement in achievement of 185 students. Suggests that the approach employed in this study would be impractical for the biology classroom. (DS)

references.title_full: Mastery Learning and Student Teams: A Factorial Experiment in Urban General Mathematics Classes
references.authors: Slavin Robert E; Karweit Nancy L;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The mathematics achievement effects of principal components of mastery learning and student team learning were evaluated in a year-long randomized experiment in urban ninth grade general mathematics classes. The components were formative tests, corrective instruction for nonmasters, summative tests (Mastery), and practice in four-member heterogeneous teams and team rewards (Teams). A 2 X 2 (Mastery by Teams) factorial experiment compared Mastery, Teams, Teams + Mastery, and a control treatment. All methods used the same materials and schedule of teaching, worksheets, and test. A nested analysis of covariance indicated significant achievement main effects for Teams but not for Mastery. No Mastery by Teams or pretest by treatment interactions were found.

references.title_full: The effects of level of cognitive achievement on selected learning criteria under mastery learning and normal classroom instruction.
references.authors: Yildiran Guzver ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The central problem of this study is "Do the two groups of students under mastery learning and normal classroom instruction who reach the same criterion level of learning as measured by an achievement test show much the same similarity on other learning criteria?" The learning criteria this study uses are the retention of the learned material on a relatively short term basis, transfer of this material to subject related novel situations, lower and higher mental processes attained or used in the process of learning, and positive affect and interest in the learning task. The research for this study was done in two settings. The micro study was done in two middle class, white Chicago area high schools, whereas the macro studies were done in four Chicago area city colleges. Each of these two settings will be discussed separately. Micro Study  this study was done in two white middle class high schools in the Chicago area, and included 5 ninth grade beginning algebra classes of 138 students. At the end of instruction the students took a final summative test on the chapter prepared by the writer of the text with the cooperation of the researcher. This test had 20 items, 15 of which were lower mental process and 5 of which were higher mental process items. The criterion level was set on these 20 items. In addition 10 items were constructed to measure transfer. A three way analysis of variance of level of learning, aptitude or time, and the kind of instruction was performed using the four learning criteria as the dependent variables. The correlations of level of learning and the learning criterion in each hypothesis, time or aptitude and the learning criterion, and finally the multiple correlations of level of learning and time or aptitude on the learning criterion for each hypothesis were obtained. When the means of the criterion groups were compared with each other on the summative test, there were no significant differences among the groups. Macro Study  this study was conducted in 4 Chicago area Junior Colleges, three of these having a majority of black students (about 90%), and one having primarily white students (about 90%). Altogether 433 students participated in the study. The subject areas included Biology 103, 111, Mathematics 103, History 103, Psychology 103, and Spanish 103. There were altogether 16 classes in the study, 8 of these were mastery learning classes, and 8 others served as control classes. The students' grade point averages were obtained as a general index of scholastic ability. Level of learning was measured by a summative test given at the end of the course. This test was composed of lower and higher mental process items. The criterion level of learning was set at 70% mastery of the material. In five of the eight studies, the mastery classes as a whole did better on their summative test scores than the control classes, in three of them significantly so. Both the results of the micro and macro studies show without a single exception that students who reach the criterion level on lower mental process items score significantly better on higher mental process items compared to students who have not reached this level.

references.title_full: A comparative study of the effects on achievement and changes in attitude of senior high school students enrolled in first year algebra under two different teaching approaches
references.authors: Englert T J;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: All students enrolled in first year algebra at Cleveland Heights High School took part In the study. Each class was to contain between twenty and twenty-five students. Each of the six classes was scheduled at a different time of the school day. All students were randomly assigned to classes by computer, with the exception of those who transferred to the school from other schools. Three pretests were administered to each of six different classes. These classes included a control and experimental class of three different teachers. The pretests Included the Cooperative Arithmetic Test, the Cooperative Structure of the Number System, and the Attitude Toward Mathematics Scale. The classes were taught using the group-orlented approach in the control classes and an individualized approach with a 70% mastery criterion in the experimental classes. All classes used the same textbook. A t test was employed on the means of the losses in raw scores from the arithmetic pretest to the algebra posttest and on the means of the gains in raw scores from the Structure of the Number System pretest to the algebra posttest. The hypothesis concerning achievement could not be rejected with respect to the groups of Teacher A and C. However, the results of the two t tests with respect to the groups of Teacher B were inconsistent. In one case a significant difference was found while no significant difference was found in the other. A t test was also used on the means of gains in raw scores from the attitude pretest to the attitude posttest. No significant differences could be found. Therefore, the hypothesis concerning attitudes could not be rejected.

references.title_full: The short-term impact of two classroom-based preventive interventions on aggressive and shy behaviors and poor achievement
references.authors: Dolan L J  Kellam S G  Brown C H  Werthamer-Larsson L   Rebok G W  Mayer L S  Laudolff J   Turkkan J S  Ford C   Wheeler L
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Two classroom-based preventive interventions were carried out on an epidemiologically defined, varied population of children in a metropolitan area in the United States. This is a report of the short-term impact and specificity of the two interventions from fall through spring of first grade. The first intervention, the Good Behavior Game, was aimed at reducing aggressive behavior and shy behavior. Aggressive behavior has been shown to be an important developmental antecedent in first grade of later delinquency and heavy drug use, particularly when coupled with shy behavior. The second intervention, Mastery Learning, was designed to improve poor reading achievement, which has been shown to be an antecedent for later depressive symptoms, as well as a correlate of aggressive and shy behaviors. Each of the two interventions had a significant and very specific impact only on its own proximal target(s). In addition to main effects, there were theoretically important variations of impacts among subgroups of children. The Good Behavior Game appeared to have a greater impact in reducing aggressive behavior among the more aggressive children. The nature of the impact of Mastery Learning differed by gender, with female high achievers benefiting more from the intervention than female low achievers, and male low achievers benefiting more than male high achievers. Developmental epidemiologically based preventive trials provide a powerful means of addressing questions about etiology and development, particularly around the issue of the malleability of developmental processes. Important questions that future work could test are whether achievement is improved by improving aggressive or shy behaviors and whether aggressive or shy behaviors are improved by improving achievement. Such investigation would inform our understanding of their etiology. © 1993.

references.title_full: The effects of individualized learning activity packages in mathematics on the academic achievement of seventh and eighth grade students in the Demopolis City School
references.authors: Stone Jr ; James Lenious ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This study investigate the effect of individualized learning activity packages in mathematics on the academic achievement of seventh- and eighth-grade students. Both seventh- and eighth-grade students in the Demopolis Junior High School had learning activity packages (LAP) provided. Each student was given a folder which contained the packages being used and each student maintained a cumulative summary of his progress, showing both the LAP covered and its level of difficulty. Conditions and performance of LAP objectives were established by the teacher and the particular learner. Students were tested for mastery before each LAP and provided with diagnostic feedback to ensure the correct level was assigned.  Post-tests designed for each difficulty level on each LAP sub-category provided the means for determining satisfactory completion of a specific learning activity package. Non-LAP instruction in mathematics consisted of the conventional lecture-discussion method with the provision of textbook exercises. The instrument used to measure the academic growth of students in LAP and non-LAP instruction in mathematics was the California Achievement Tests, 1970 edition.  The four control variables used in matching students were  (1) chronological age, (2) sex, (3) race, and (4) intelligence quotient. On this basis, fifty-eight students were matched so as to provide twenty-nine pairs. Twelve pairs (n = 24) comprised the seventh-grade sample and seventeen pairs (n = 34) made up the eighth-grade sample. Analysis of variance was utilized in looking for significant differences in academic achievement between the two treatments at each of the two grade levels. An examination of treatment means revealed that in grade eight students undergoing conventional classroom instruction consistently had a mean greater than those utilizing Learning Activity Packages. In no case was such a difference statistically significant at .05. By levels in grade eight, there were no statistically significant differences at .05. Treatment means in grade seven indicated that students achieved greater academic growth in LAP than in conventional classroom instruction. At no time, however, were differences significant at .05. No F values were significant at .05 in relation to levels nor to interaction (treatments x levels) in grade seven.

references.title_full: A study of the effect of different approaches to the teaching of vocabulary on reading achievement and vocabulary development at the fifth grade level.
references.authors: Halliwell D D;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The basic design of this experiment was the nonequivalent control group design. There were three fifth grade classes in the Experimental I treatment, three in the Experimental II treatment and three in the control treatment. These nine classes were randomly selected from fourteen fifth grade classes in six schools and randomly assigned to treatment groups. The subjects in this study were children of nine fifth grade classes from six schools in the Cortland Public School System, Cortland, New York. Class size varied from 19 to 30 students. At the time of pretesting there were 209 children included in the experiment. Due to attrition, this sample dwindled to 185 when the final data were collected. Therefore, in this study only the pre and posttest scores of the final 185 subjects were used in the data analysis. Experimental I - (IVD) - the children in this group followed the treatment labeled Individual Vocabulary Development (IVD). The children worked on their vocabulary exercises individually with assistance from the teacher if needed to achieve mastery. Experimental II - (PGIVD) - the children in this group followed the treatment labeled Peer Group Interaction Vocabulary Development (PGIVD). These children worked on their self-directing and self-correcting vocabulary exercises in groups of twos, threes, or fours formed within the confines of the three vocabulary levels to achieve mastery. Control Treatment - (RCPVD) - The children in this group followed the regular classroom procedure for Vocabulary development, and is therefore labeled RCPVD. The entire Cortland School System uses the Lippincott Readers as the main basal series. Reading achievement was measured by the Gates MacGinitie Reading Test, Survey D, Form-M administered as a pretest. Growth in reading achievement was measured by Form 2-M of the same instrument, administered as a posttest. There were no significant differences among any of the three treatment groups in vocabulary, comprehension or total reading posttest means on the Gates-McGinitie Reading Test at the end of the experiment.

references.title_full: The design and evaluation of an individualized, contract-directed high school chemistry course
references.authors: Carlson John Allen;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: A posttest-only, control group design was chosen for this study with random assignment of subjects. The individualized, contract-directed high school chemistry, course was characterized by the following  individual and small group activities, student self-pacing, which included teacher indicated minimum acceptable requirements, unit behavioral objectives citing multiple references, PACE learning packets for each unit that directed student day-to-day activities, PACE unit pretests, tape-recorded and printed unit summaries that assisted the student with content Integration, audio-visual experiment previews, student tutoring and team learning, topic-related seminars, lectures and demonstrations presented upon student request, investigator-designed supplementary materials for teacher-directed remedial action, topic-related full-length films and film loops, a quantity/quality grading system, and an underlying mastery learning philosophy. Standardized and unbiased administrative procedures were used to assign forty-four students to second period chemistry classes and forty-six students to third period classes.  The significant treatment effect demonstrated on the Semester Two Examination favored the control groups' students over the experimental groups' students. The significant treatment and academic ability interaction demonstrated on the Tennessee Self-Concept Scale favored the experimental middle academic ability groups' students over the control groups' middle academic ability students. The significant treatment and academic ability interaction demonstrated on the Semester One Examination favored the middle academic ability control groups' students over the experimental groups' middle academic ability students.

references.title_full: A comparison of the effectiveness of two methods of presenting science experiments to children of the fourth grade in a northeastern suburb.
references.authors: Netburn Allan N;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The study describes the effectiveness of teaching as prescribed by the Conceptually Oriented Program in Elementary Science (COPES) program compared to an audio-tutorial approach at the fourth grade level. The experimental group covered the COPES content but with audio-tutorial materials prepared by the investigator. No significant differences were found between the achievement scores of the experimental subjects and control subjects. A significant difference existed between the amount of time spent by the two groups on the sequence of activities. Children in the experimental group took significantly less time to complete the activities. (PS)

references.title_full: Mathematics Mastery: Primary Evaluation Report
references.authors: Vignoles Anna ; Jerrim John ; Cowan Richard ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The Mathematics Mastery programme is a whole-school approach to teaching mathematics that aims to raise attainment for all pupils and close the attainment gap between pupils from low income families and their peers. The programme aims to deepen pupils’ understanding of key mathematical concepts. Compared to traditional curricula, fewer topics are covered in more depth and greater emphasis is placed on problem solving and on encouraging mathematical thinking. This evaluation assessed the impact of Mathematics Mastery on pupils in Year 1, after the programme had been implemented in schools for one year. It was intended that schools would also begin to use the programme in Year 2 in the second year of implementation, and continue until the approach was in place across the school. Eighty-three schools from London and the South East participated in the trial, with a total sample of 4,176 pupils. Participating schools received training and resources to support the adoption of the programme which was delivered by the education charity Ark.

references.authors: Thomas Buren G;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purpose of this study was to compare the achievement and attitude toward mathematics of students in continuous progress advanced algebra classes with the achievement of students in the traditional advanced algebra classes.    Five teachers were involved, with two teachers teaching a total of five sections of continuous progress advanced algebra and three teachers teaching a total of five sections of traditional advanced algebra. All of the students were given pretests in achievement and attitude toward mathematics in September, 1969. They were given the same two tests as posttests when they finished the course.   Student achievement in the continuous progress classes was not significantly different from student achievement in the traditional classes as measured by the Cooperative Mathematics Test, Algebra II, Form A.

references.title_full: A comparison of learning outcomes in CBA chemistry when group and individualized instruction techniques are employed.
references.authors: Krockover Gerald Howard;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Grade 10 students using the Chemical Bond Approach (CBA) materials in a typical classroom setting with large group instruction were compared with students in an "individualized" class using a laboratory-centered, self-paced approach. Both groups were initially comparable with respect to grade nine scores on the "Iowa Test of Educational Development". Students in the individualized class rated their teacher significantly higher than students in the larger group, and stated that their ability to organize their work increased. The scores of the two groups of students were not significantly different on the following tests  "American Chemical Society Cooperative Examination-General Chemistry", "Test on Understanding Science, Watson-Glaser Critical Thinking Appraisal", the "Prouse Subject Preference", six CBA achievement tests, and the final examination. (Author/AL)

references.title_full: A comparison of mastery learning feedback systems, affecting achievement in chemistry
references.title_parent: The Annual Meeting of the American Educational Research Association (ERIC Document Rekoduction Service No. ED 139 650)
references.authors: Swanson D H;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The effectiveness of a Keller and Bloom mastery learning program for high school science students was examined by comparing remediation strategies of both programs and that of a traditional strategy. The data gathered in the experiment in chemistry were from a pre- and post-achievement test. Cognitive achievement was statistically different (p < .025). Additional analysis revealed the greatest difference was between a Bloom and a traditional strategy. Gain score analyses failed to produce any significant differences. A Chi-square analysis of the number of objectives achieved produced significant values of .004 and .034, respectively, for the Keller and Bloom groups over the traditional group.

references.title_full: Mastery Learning and Student Teams: A Factorial Experiment in Urban General Mathematics Classes
references.authors: Slavin Robert E; Karweit Nancy L;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The mathematics achievement effects of principal components of mastery learning and student team learning were evaluated in a year-long randomized experiment in urban ninth grade general mathematics classes. The components were formative tests, corrective instruction for nonmasters, summative tests (Mastery), and practice in four-member heterogeneous teams and team rewards (Teams). A 2 X 2 (Mastery by Teams) factorial experiment compared Mastery, Teams, Teams + Mastery, and a control treatment. All methods used the same materials and schedule of teaching, worksheets, and test. A nested analysis of covariance indicated significant achievement main effects for Teams but not for Mastery. No Mastery by Teams or pretest by treatment interactions were found.

references.title_full: Consequences of Training Teachers to Use a Mastery Learning Strategy
references.authors: Okey James R;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purpose of this project was to produce materials that would foster favorable teacher attitudes toward the philosophy behind mastery learning. One other purpose was to help teachers acquire the skills needed to use mastery learning in their classrooms and to determine the effects on pupils when mastery learning techniques were used. Forty-four teachers and interns from four Indianapolis schools were equally divided into groups according to race and sex. The material developed was a Mastery Teaching module which included an introduction and six sections. A slide/tape accompanied each of the seven parts. An accompanying manual contained objectives, practice exercises, and feedback. The manual also included self-tests with answers for each section, a pre-test on prerequisites, and a project section. Pre- and post-treatment measures were administered to the teachers and interns on both cognitive and affective variables. The results indicated that teachers and interns acquired the mastery teaching skills and, used them to the degree that pupils perceived differences in their teaching. Teacher attitudes toward the mastery teaching philosophy were generally positive, and students' attitudes and achievement were favorably altered because of their teachers' use of mastery teaching. (DT)

All students were randomly assigned to classes by computer, with the exception of those who transferred to the school from other schools. Three pretests were administered to each of six different classes. These classes included a control and experimental class of three different teachers. The pretests Included the Cooperative Arithmetic Test, the Cooperative Structure of the Number System, and the Attitude Toward Mathematics Scale. references.title_full: Student Teams and Mastery Learning: A Factorial Experiment in Urban Math Nine Classes.
references.authors: Slavin Robert E; Karweit Nancy L;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Mastery Learning and Student Team Learning are two widely used instructional methods designed to confront the problem of student diversity in group-paced instruction. This study evaluated Mastery Learning, Student Team Learning, and a combination, in 43 inner-city math nine classes over a full school year. Results indicated greater achievement on a standardized test for Team classes than non-Team classes, but no greater achievement in Mastery than non-Mastery classes. Differences in time use were suggested to explain treatment differences in student achievement. (Author/MP)

references.title_full: The effects of level of cognitive achievement on selected learning criteria under mastery learning and normal classroom instruction.
references.authors: Yildiran Guzver ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The central problem of this study is "Do the two groups of students under mastery learning and normal classroom instruction who reach the same criterion level of learning as measured by an achievement test show much the same similarity on other learning criteria?" The learning criteria this study uses are the retention of the learned material on a relatively short term basis, transfer of this material to subject related novel situations, lower and higher mental processes attained or used in the process of learning, and positive affect and interest in the learning task.  The research for this study was done in two settings. The micro study was done in two middle class, white Chicago area high schools, whereas the macro studies were done in four Chicago area city colleges. Each of these two settings will be discussed separately.  Micro Study  this study was done in two white middle class high schools in the Chicago area, and included 5 ninth grade beginning algebra classes of 138 students. At the end of instruction  the students took a final summative test on the chapter prepared by the writer of the text with the cooperation of the researcher. This test had 20 items, 15 of which were lower mental process and 5 of which were higher mental process items. The criterion level was set on these 20 items. In addition 10 items were constructed to measure transfer. A three way analysis of variance of level of learning, aptitude or time, and the kind of instruction was performed using the four learning criteria as the dependent variables. The correlations of level of learning and the learning criterion in each hypothesis, time or aptitude and the learning criterion, and finally the multiple correlations of level of learning and time or aptitude on the learning criterion for each hypothesis were obtained.  When the means of the criterion groups were compared with each other on the summative test, there were no significant differences among the groups. Macro Study  this study was conducted in 4 Chicago area Junior Colleges, three of these having a majority of black students (about 90%), and one having primarily white students (about 90%). Altogether 433 students participated in the study. The subject areas included Biology 103, 111, Mathematics 103, History 103, Psychology 103, and Spanish 103. There were altogether 16 classes in the study, 8 of these were mastery learning classes, and 8 others served as control classes.  The students' grade point averages were obtained as a general index of scholastic ability.  Level of learning was measured by a summative test given at the end of the course. This test was composed of lower and higher mental process items. The criterion level of learning was set at 70% mastery of the material. In five of the eight studies, the mastery classes as a whole did better on their summative test scores than the control classes, in three of them significantly so.  Both the results of the micro and macro studies show without a single exception that students who reach the criterion level on lower mental process items score significantly better on higher mental process items compared to students who have not reached this level.

references.title_full: An investigation of the effectiveness of certain scheduling procedures on mathematical achievement of junior high school pupils.
references.authors: Cohen Louis S;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This investigation compared the relative effectiveness of three plans of junior high school organization on measurements of educational development and attitude using as criterion measures the grade level equivalent scores from the Modern Math Understanding Tests and weighted raw scores from the Minnesota Attitude Inventory Scale.  The Olson school day consisted of sixteen time modules of twenty-five minutes each. Students' and teachers' schedules cycled or repeated weekly. Group sixes, modes of instruction, and allocation of spaces varied considerably from the traditional format with an underlying mastery approach. The traditional Portland school day consisted of six time periods of fifty-five minutes each. Students' and teachers' schedules were constant day to day. The mathematics periods were for the most part for independent study or small group presentations. There was no difference in mean achievement, as measured by the Modern Math Understanding Test, between students taught under the modular plan and students taught under the traditional plan.  The mean score of the modular group exceeded that of the traditional group only in the high ability level and that by only one month. For the middle and low ability groups, the traditional group scored higher by five and one month, respectively.

references.title_full: Effects of Learning with Cooperative-Mastery Method on Elementary Students
references.authors: Mevarech Z R; Susak Z ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The present study examined the effects of the cooperative-mastery method and each of its components on children's questioning behavior, creativity, and achievement. A 2 × 2 (Cooperative x Mastery) factorial study compared the cognitive performances of pupus who were trained to generate questions under cooperative learning (CL), mastery learning (ML), cooperative-mastery learning (CML), and a control treatment. Participants were 271 third and fourth-grade pupils. Intact classes within each grade level were randomly assigned to one of the four treatment groups. Results showed that CML and ML pupils scored higher on measures of higher order questioning skills and originality than did the CL group, who, in turn, scored higher than the control group. The educational implications of the study are discussed. © 1993 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

references.title_full: A strategy of mastery learning in fifth grade arithmetic
references.authors: Kersh M E;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The Carroll Model of school learning provides a conceptual design of variables affecting success in school learning. The Bloom mastery learning strategy proposes a sequence of steps which together encompass the variables of the Carroll Model and is, then, one implementation of this model. The present study attempted to apply the Bloom strategy in fifth grade classes in the subject of mathematics for one school year. Could this Bloom strategy be effective for a school year (nine months) in a regular curriculum content area for elementary students? Moreover, since there exists a deficit in learning among students of lower-socio-economic classes in relation to students of middle-socio-economic classes, school instruction may influence the achievement of groups of students in various ways. Would the Bloom strategy be equally effective when used in the classes of two different socio-economic communities? These two questions constituted the major focus of this study. Using the pre-test scores on the two Stanford Achievement sub-tests (Concepts and Applications) and the pre-test scores on the Mastery Criterion Test as covariates, an analysis of covariance produced no significant interaction on post-test scores between socio-economic class and treatment. It is clear that the experimental classes did not differ significantly from the control classes, nor did the Community L classes differ from the previous year's class on achievement scores. However, in Community M, the experimental classes did attain mastery of the mastery criterion in greater numbers and to a significantly higher degree than their previous year control classes. The time series study shows no increased learning rate for experimental classes of Community l-1 on the Stanford Applications sub-test, nor any increase for the Stanford Concepts sub-test. On the basis of data we conclude that the results are inconclusive with respect to the main study hypothesis.

references.title_full: Independent instruction in high school chemistry: A comparison with a traditional technique
references.authors: Braly Joe Lee;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purpose of the study was to determine differences in chemistry resulting from a traditional and an independent technique of teaching. The population included four chemistry classes at Scottsdale Saguaro High School. Intact groups were assigned to experimental or control groups by random processes. The control group was presented the CHEM Study program in essentially a lecture-laboratory manner using the teacher's guide and its suggestions for instruction. The experimental group was permitted to study, or not study, the same material during class periods with no direct instruction by the teacher except in a tutorial manner. Pretest and posttest measures were obtained using the ACS-NSTA Chemistry Examination. A statistical analysis revealed no significant differences in chemistry achievement between the control and the experimental groups. The author concluded that within the expressed and implied limitations of the study  (1) chemistry can be taught by either a traditional technique or an independent study technique, resulting in approximately the same amount of achievement  and (2) achievement alone does not provide enough information relative to deciding whether an independent study or traditional technique should be used in teaching chemistry at the high school level. (Author/MLH)
