references.title_full: Interclass Grouping for Reading Instruction
references.authors: Moorhouse William F;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: During the first three years of elementary school, the range in reading level among pupils becomes wider and wider. It is common to find five to seven reading levels represented by the pupils in a fourth-grade class. In February, 1958, an experiment was begun in two public elementary schools of Laramie, Wyoming, to determine whether interclass grouping for reading in Grades 4, 5, and 6 would produce readers superior to those grouped conventionally by grade levels for reading. The experiment was evaluated at the end of one semester, at the end of three semesters, and again after five semesters.

references.title_full: Best Practice in Grouping Students Intervention B : Mixed Attainment Grouping Pilot report and executive summary
references.authors: Roy Palak ; Styles Ben ; Walker Matt ; Bradshaw Sally ; Nelson Julie ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The Best Practice in Mixed Attainment (BPMA) intervention trained schools to adopt best practice mixed attainment approaches to grouping Year 7 and Year 8 students for English and mathematics in order to raise attainment. Schools were expected to create classes that contained pupils with a wide range of Key Stage 2 national curriculum results in English and mathematics. Teachers were trained to communicate high expectations of all pupils and to use flexible within class grouping and differentiation techniques. They were asked to minimise the use of marks levels and grades, and to provide formative feedback through comments instead, with a view to creating a growth mindset in pupils. The intervention was developed by a team now based at UCL Institute of Education. The intervention was developed with three schools between September 2014 and July 2015 and piloted with a further eight intervention schools through a pilot randomised controlled trial (RCT) starting in September 2015 and following Year 7 students for two academic years. The trial was funded by the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF). The aim of the pilot trial was to help inform decisions about a future large-scale RCT and to identify barriers to adopting mixed ability teaching. Preliminary outcome data was collected in order to rehearse for a future trial.

references.title_full: The Effectiveness Of Ability Grouping In General Science Classes
references.authors: Platz Eugene Freeland;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: It was the purpose of this study (1) to compare the effect of ability grouping on the academic performance of ninth grade science students  and (2) to determine if a relationship exists between ability grouped and ungrouped students with regard to certain understandings, interests, and classroom performance in ninth grade science classes. Two hundred sixty-two students were grouped at three approximate levels  above average, with CTMM scores of 140-116  average, with CTM 4 scores of 115-96  and below average, with CTMM scores of 95-78. These students were then assigned to grouped and ungrouped classes and matched as nearly as possible according to eighth grade science marks, interest, age, and sex. The teacher variable was controlled by assigning each teacher five classes  two ability grouped, and three ungrouped. Academic achievement was measured by performance on the Discovery and Progress Science 3 Examination and by grades at the first and second marking periods. An attempt to discover whether the broad objectives of science were being met was made by gathering student responses to a questionnaire, and certain understandings regarding science were ascertained from data from the Test of Understanding Science distributed by the Educational Testing Service. Student classroom performance was measured by a teacher rating card. The data were treated using the t-score and chi square techniques and inferences were made on the basis of the statistical treatment. Based on the findings of this study 1. For increased student achievement on examinations, ability grouping of below-average students is more effective than the ungrouped system of classroom organization. Neither the grouped nor the ungrouped system of classroom organization is more effective for above-average and average students for the purpose of increased student achievement on examinations, nor is there any difference in the effectiveness of being grouped or ungrouped at any level where the purpose of grouping is student attainment of higher academic marks. 2. There is little relationship between being grouped and ungrouped in ninth grade general science and classroom performance, attendance, behavior, and citizenship as measured by teachers' ratings. Grouped systems of classroom organization may tend to result in more behavior problems than in ungrouped systems as noted by the number of guidance office referrals. 3. Student attitudes, interests, and understandings related to the broad objectives of general science are not influenced by types of classroom organization compared in this study. 4. There is little difference between being grouped or ungrouped when consideration is given to general science and certain understandings of science as measured by a standardized instrument.

references.title_full: Ability Grouping And Its Effect Upon Individual Achievement
references.authors: Loomer Bradley Max A X;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate one specific type of homogeneous grouping. The grouping procedure employed in this investigation centered around careful consideration of such factors as intelligence quotient, mental age, chronological age, reading achievement level, composite rating of a standardized basic skills test, teacher appraisal of ability, sex, and the school administrator's judgment. Each pupil in grades four, five, and six was categorized as belonging to one of five ability levels designated bright, above average, average, below average, and low by the principals, teachers, and the writer. In schools where there was more than one section per grade these levels were used as the basis for sectioning. In one class section were placed all pupils, of a specific grade, who were identified as belonging to the bright ability level. In another section, separate from the one containing the bright pupils, the pupils identified as belonging to the low ability class were placed. Grouped along with the bright ability level pupils were other students of the same grade who were identified as belonging to the ability levels designated as above average, average, and below average.  The results of this analysis verified that all heterogeneous classes encompassed pupils from all five ability levels. For each pupil in the study the following information was collected  a) IQ  b) Grade  c ) Age  d) Mental Age  f ) Iowa Tests of Basic Skills for all areas of the test ( i.e. Vocabulary, Reading, Language, Work Study, Arithmetic , and Composite.) This study devoted itself to the overall group comparisons between those students in the homogeneous and heterogeneous classes who were identified as belonging to the same ability levels. To test the significance between all group comparisons the F statistic using analysis of variance procedures was employed. The results, in general, do not lend support to the claimed advantage of grouping as opposed to no grouping. The evidence presented seems to indicate that pupils, for the most part, are not affected by the administrative procedure commonly described as homogeneous grouping. The fact that the homogeneous classes did not achieve significantly more than did the heterogeneous classes does not automatically rule out any advantages to the grouping procedure. It may well be that the instructional task was made easier by having the extremely bright in one room and the extremely low in another room. The evidence presented in this study indicates no decided advantage of this method of grouping over a random method of assigning pupils to classes. The evidence seems to indicate that grouping is merely an administrative device employed to serve the schools in assigning pupils to classes. If there are advantages accruing to this procedure, they must be found in areas other than those measurable by a standardized test of basic skills. The key to good education of children evidently rests with good teaching. This study points this out by showing that the grouping procedure does not by and in itself produce greater gains by students, at least those in grades four, five, and six.

references.authors: Burris Carol Corbett; Heubert Jay P; Levin Henry M;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This longitudinal study examined the effects of providing an accelerated mathematics curriculum in heterogeneously grouped middle school classes in a diverse suburban school district. A quasi-experimental cohort design was used to evaluate subsequent completion of advanced high school math courses as well as academic achievement. Results showed that probability of completion of advanced math courses increased significantly and markedly in all groups, including minority students, students of low socioeconomic status, and students at all initial achievement levels. Also, the performance of initial high achievers did not differ statistically in heterogeneous classes relative to previous homogeneous grouping, and rates of participation in advanced placement calculus and test scores improved.

references.title_full: A Comparison of Pupil Achievement after One and One-Half and Three Years in a Nongraded Program
references.authors: Jones Charles ; Moore William ; Devender Frank Van;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Effects of nongraded organization on reading performance of elementary pupils were assessed at the end of one and one-half school years and three years to determine If non-grading resulted in differences in performance, and if differences were stable after nongrading became an established part of the school organization. Teachers (N = 0) and pupils (N = 52) were randomly assigned to E (nungraded) and C (graded) groups. Teachers of both groups received Identical treatment  workshops, consultant services, and materials. Reading performance of 13 group was significantly higher (p .01) at end of eighteen months, but there were no significant differences at end of three years. Differences in results may be due to transient effects of experimental conditions or greater suitability of nongraded organisation for beginning students.

references.title_full: An Evaluation Of Ability Grouping In Ninth Grade English
references.authors: Barton Dean Preston;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purpose of this study was an attempt to evaluate the practices of ability grouping in ninth grade English classes taught at a Utah junior high school and to determine teacher, student, and parent attitudes toward ability grouping. Students were divided into an experimental and control group based upon performance in eighth grade English. There were 115 experimental group students, who were subdivided into 4 homogenous classrooms, while 114 control group students were heterogeneously grouped into 4 English classes. All students in this study were given standardized tests at the be¬ginning and the end of the school year. From school records, informa-tion was obtained concerning citizenship marks, scholarship marks, and daily attendance. Twenty-five spelling words were given to each ninth-grade student and corrected by the writer. The following day the tests were handed back unmarked to the owners who were then asked to correct and score their own papers. The writer’s and the owners’ scores were compared to determine evidence of cheating. Finally, an attitude questionnaire was developed and used to determine teachers' and parents' attitudes toward ability grouping. The major conclusion derived from this study seems to be that random grouping is as effective as homogeneous grouping for all ninth grade English students when effectiveness is measured by English achievement, average daily attendance, citizenship marks, scholarship marks, the number of underachievers, and lessening of pressures to cheat. However, English teachers believe that thy do a more effective teaching job when the range of the class abilities is reduced.

references.title_full: The effects of three types of grouping on achievement
references.authors: Baiow Irving H; Ruddell Arden K;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This study was designed to compare growth in achievement between homogeneous, cluster, and heterogeneous plans for grouping by three different intelligence levels of children in ten different facets of the elementary school curriculum. Questions of specific concern to this study were  Which of the plans for grouping (homogeneous, cluster, or heterogeneous) appears to be most conducive to growth in achievement as measured by the Metropolitan Achievement Tests? Is the achievement of any ability level (high I.Q., middle I.Q. or low I.Q.) in various facets of the elementary curriculum affected by the grouping plan employed?

references.title_full: Grouping of the Gifted: An Experimental Approach.
references.authors: Bent Leo G;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: While in 3rd grade, 487 students were selected for placement in special classes for the gifted from grades 4 through 8. Teachers of the special classes were chosen by school administrators. Their teaching experience averaged 9 years, and eight held advanced degrees. Sixteen attended special summer programs on the gifted and were given inservice assistance. Results indicated that the program children equalled or surpassed the controls in academic achievement as measured by standardized tests despite the fact that their supplementary enriching activities reduced by about one half the time spent on regular classroom activities. Further results indicated skill in foreign language, research, and critical thinking as well as growth in social awareness and concern, leadership, creativity, interests, and self reliance in school activities. Approval of the program by both teachers and parents was noted. (Author/JD)

references.title_full: Peer effects, teacher incentives, and the impact of tracking: Evidence from a randomized evaluation in Kenya
references.authors: Duflo E ; Dupas P ; Kremer M ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: To the extent that students benefit from high-achieving peers, tracking will help strong students and hurt weak ones. However, all students may benefit if tracking allows teachers to better tailor their instruction level. Lower-achieving pupils are particularly likely to benefit from tracking when teachers have incentives to teach to the top of the distribution. We propose a simple model nesting these effects and test its implications in a randomized tracking experiment conducted with 121 primary schools in Kenya. While the direct effect of high-achieving peers is positive, tracking benefited lower-achieving pupils indirectly by allowing teachers to teach to their level.

references.title_full: A Study Of The Effect Of Inter-Class Ability Grouping On Achievement In Reading
references.authors: Moses Paul James;
references.institution: Louisiana State University and Agricultural & Mechanical College
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of inter-class ability grouping on the reading achievement of elementary students. Experimental and control classes were set up in grades four, five, and six in School District Twenty- Two of Calcasieu Parish. A total of twenty-seven experimental classes was established in the three grades. These twenty-seven classes consisted of nine each of high, average, and low ability levels. Four hundred fifty students, fifty at each ability level of each of the three grades, were selected at random from the experimental classes and paired with other students attending homogeneous classes in School District Twenty-Two. The students selected for the experimental classes were paired with other students in the same grade, according to sex, age, Stanford Achievement Reading Test scores, and California Mental Maturity Test scores. Teachers for the different levels of the experimental groups were selected by lot from the teaching staff previously assigned to that particular school and grade. The same supervisory services and instructional materials were provided for the experimental and control groups. A second Stanford Achievement Test was administered at the end of the semester to all students used in the study. The results obtained from these tests were tabulated and the gains made in reading achievement were analyzed. The t-test was used to test for significance of the difference in mean grade placement gains in each group. The difference in mean gains was not found to be significant at the .05 level for any of the three ability levels. On the basis of the evidence presented.in this study, it is indicated that the reading achievement of elementary students is not significantly affected when inter-class ability grouping is practiced.

references.title_full: Differentiated Multi-Track Grouping Versus Uni-Track Educational Grouping In Mathematics
references.authors: Adamson DP ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The major purpose of this study was to compare the arithmetic achievement gains of seventh and eighth grade students placed in an experimental program consisting of high, middle and low ability groups having different materials and objectives for each of the three levels of students, against a conventional uni-track program employing heterogeneous grouping.  The analysis of variance was used to determine if differences existed between the groups. To analyze the interaction between the low ability group, the middle group, and the high ability group, the Newman-Keuls Sequential Range Test was used. Tables showing the level means were constructed as an aid in the analysis of the two and three- way interactions.  There was no significant difference between the mean achievement gains of the students placed in groups on the basis of their ability and those of students grouped heterogeneously. The reduction of certified personnel with teacher aides used in their place did not produce results significantly different from those coming from the control school.

references.title_full: A study of the effects of the use of vertical reading ability groupings for reading classes as compared with heterogeneous groupings in grades four, five, and six in the Port Huron Area Schools of Michigan over a three-year period.
references.authors: DeGrow G S;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The problem concerning the improvement of reading instruction at the later elementary level was defined for the research study as follows  Will the use of vertical ability grouping over a three-year period in reading classes for grades four, five, and six in the Port Huron Area Schools of Michigan result in significantly different achievement for those groups as compared to classes grouped heterogeneously? The research design was established in three parts  I. A One-Year study of a Ten Percent Random sample from an experimental group of 1200 students in grades 4, 5, and 6 grouped vertically for reading, matched according to intelligence quotient, grade level, sex, and reading grade score with an equal number of students from a control group of 690 students grouped heterogeneously according to regular grade level. II. A Four-Year Cross-Sectional Comparison of intelligence quotient and reading scores of sixth-grade students during the two years prior to the grouping experiment and the first two years of the experiment. III. A Three-Year ten longitudinal Comparison of the reading test records of 100 students who were enrolled in the experimental reading program in grades 4, 5, and 6. Results are reported and discussed.

references.title_full: Evaluation Of A Vertical-Horizontal Enrichment Program For The Math-Gifted Students Fourth, Fifth And Sixth Grades.
references.authors: Koukeyan Berjouhi B;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: In an attempt to determine and organize an effective mathematics program for the most capable students in mathematics, Pasadena Unified School District designed a vertical-horizontal enrichment program. In this study the vertical-horizontal enrichment program was set up by combining the techniques of homogeneous grouping and providing differentiation of assignments through enriched curriculum opportunities. The purpose of this study was to determine if a significant difference existed in arithmetic achievement and in attitude toward arithmetic among mathematically-gifted students who participated in a vertical-horizontal program and similarly mathematically gifted students who did not receive such instruction. The 121 students in the experimental schools participated in a vertical-horizontal enrichment program in three elementary schools and the 94 students in the three control schools did not receive such instruction. Significantly greater gains were made on the CTBS by the fourth graders in the experimental group than in the control group both in arithmetic computation and total arithmetic (P <.04 and P ^ .005). There were no significant differences between the treatment groups in gains in the Concepts and Application subtests. No significant differences existed between the treatment groups in any of the subtests of the CTBS at the fifth grade level. Negative adjusted gains were obtained in the raw scores with regard to all the subtests. In the analysis involving arithmetic achievement on the CTBS for the sixth grade, both groups showed gains with the means of the experimental group being higher as compared to the control group, but none of the means reached levels of significance.

references.title_full: Ability Grouping And Its Effect Upon Individual Achievement
references.authors: Loomer Bradley Max A X;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate one specific type of homogeneous grouping. The grouping procedure employed in this investigation centered around careful consideration of such factors as intelligence quotient, mental age, chronological age, reading achievement level, composite rating of a standardized basic skills test, teacher appraisal of ability, sex, and the school administrator's judgment. Each pupil in grades four, five, and six was categorized as belonging to one of five ability levels designated bright, above average, average, below average, and low by the principals, teachers, and the writer. In schools where there was more than one section per grade these levels were used as the basis for sectioning. In one class section were placed all pupils, of a specific grade, who were identified as belonging to the bright ability level. In another section, separate from the one containing the bright pupils, the pupils identified as belonging to the low ability class were placed. Grouped along with the bright ability level pupils were other students of the same grade who were identified as belonging to the ability levels designated as above average, average, and below average.  The results of this analysis verified that all heterogeneous classes encompassed pupils from all five ability levels. For each pupil in the study the following information was collected  a) IQ  b) Grade  c ) Age  d) Mental Age  f ) Iowa Tests of Basic Skills for all areas of the test ( i.e. Vocabulary, Reading, Language, Work Study, Arithmetic , and Composite.) This study devoted itself to the overall group comparisons between those students in the homogeneous and heterogeneous classes who were identified as belonging to the same ability levels. To test the significance between all group comparisons the F statistic using analysis of variance procedures was employed. The results, in general, do not lend support to the claimed advantage of grouping as opposed to no grouping. The evidence presented seems to indicate that pupils, for the most part, are not affected by the administrative procedure commonly described as homogeneous grouping. The fact that the homogeneous classes did not achieve significantly more than did the heterogeneous classes does not automatically rule out any advantages to the grouping procedure. It may well be that the instructional task was made easier by having the extremely bright in one room and the extremely low in another room. The evidence presented in this study indicates no decided advantage of this method of grouping over a random method of assigning pupils to classes. The evidence seems to indicate that grouping is merely an administrative device employed to serve the schools in assigning pupils to classes. If there are advantages accruing to this procedure, they must be found in areas other than those measurable by a standardized test of basic skills. The key to good education of children evidently rests with good teaching. This study points this out by showing that the grouping procedure does not by and in itself produce greater gains by students, at least those in grades four, five, and six.

references.authors: Fogelman Ken ; Essen Juliet ; Tibbenham Alan ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Of course, when the Secretaries of State (DES, 1977) wrote the above they had in mind the selection of children to go to a particular type of school, and in this narrow context the statement is true. However, the importance of this change could be illusory if divisions between schools have merely been replaced by selective systems within the schools. Downey & Kelly (1975), for example, have argued that comprehensive education cannot" be undertaken without fundamental re-appraisal of the internal reorganization of the school.

references.title_full: Achievement in eighth grade science by heterogeneous and homogeneous classes
references.authors: Bicak Laddie J;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: TODAY our schools are making a greater effort than ever before to educate all of our youth within the limits of individual capabilities, at all levels of formal education. Among the techniques being employed by schools to provide for individual differences are those involving homogeneous grouping. Homogeneous grouping is a broad term which includes such forms of grouping as ability grouping, interest grouping, grouping according to physical characteristics, or many other criteria. The purpose of the application test designed for this study was to determine whether there was a significant difference between the experimental (homogeneous) and control (heterogeneous) sections in their ability to utilize and apply meteorological information. The application test (reliability .80), employed the use of materials with which a pupil might come in daily contact. The material for the items was obtained from such sources as 2x2 color slides of cloud formations, articles with reference to weather found in current newspapers and popular periodicals, and weather forecast maps as illustrated in daily newspapers.

references.title_full: A longitudinal study of the effectiveness of the track plan in the secondary schools of a metropolitan community
references.authors: Kline RE ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Four schools were selected with a total sample of 798 students (364 control and 434 experimental), comparing tracked and untracked classes across ten currlculum areas using Iowa Test of Educational development. ANOVA was used to ascertain significant differences in achievement between the control and experimental tracks. The analysis yielded overall non-significant results.

references.title_full: A study of the effectiveness of ability grouping on success in first year algebra
references.authors: Bailey HP ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The objectives of this investigation are as follows  (1) To determine if there is a significant difference in achievement, in first year algebra, between Track I students in homogeneous classes and Track I students in heterogeneous classes as measured by raw score gain on the Lankton First-Year Algebra Test and teachers’ final grades. (2) To determine if there is a significant difference in achievement, in first year algebra, between Track II students in homogeneous classes and Track II students in heterogeneous classes as measured by raw score gain on the Lankton First-Year Algebra Test and teachers’ final grades. (3) To determine whether there is a significant track, mixed homogeneous, interaction regression and teacher effect as determined by raw score gain on the Lankton First-Year Algebra Test and teachers’ final grades. (4) To determine the extent to which success in first year algebra is related to success in first year geometry as measured by terminal raw scores on the Lankton First-Year Algebra and Shaycoft Plane Geometry Tests and teachers’ final grades in the two subjects.

references.title_full: Inter-Class Grouping for Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Grades
references.authors: Russell David H;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: For some years the San Francisco Public Schools have used a system of grouping for reading instruction in the intermediate grades locally known as "circling." Instead of the more usual grouping within anyone class, "circling" means that a considerable number of pupils in grades 4, 5, and 6 actually change rooms and teachers during reading periods. The different classes divide into three groups of high, average, and low reading abilities. Fourth-grade pupils of high reading achievement may move to a fifth or even sixth-grade group  the fifth-grade pupils may go into the slower group of fourth-grade or less achievement, stay in their own class, or move up into the group of best readers with sixth grade or better reading ability  sixth-grade pupils may move down one or two classes or stay with the group of best readers. The present investigation evaluates this attempt to provide for individual differences in reading ability by a study of comparable pupil achievement on standardized tests and the opinions of elementary school principals who have had both regular class grouping and inter-class grouping in their school.

references.title_full: The Effect Of Grouping On Achievement And Attitudes Toward Learning Of First Grade Pupils
references.authors: Flair Merrel Dean;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This experimental study dealt with two approaches to grouping first grade pupils for instruction. Specifically, the study sought to determine whether there was any significant difference in reading achievement, arithmetic achievement and attitudes toward learning between children who were grouped by ability and those who were randomly assigned to classes. Four of seventeen first grade classes in a suburban school district were designated as "high," "middle" or "low." Each pupil in the school which housed the homogeneously grouped classes was assigned to the appropriate class on the basis of the kindergarten teacher's judgment of his potential academic success. This teacher judgment was made by predicting whether the child would be in the upper quarter, middle one-half, or lower quarter of his first grade class as regards success in reading and arithmetic. There was no attempt to differentiate among the pupils in the middle 50 per cent and thus there were two "middle" classes, one "high" class, and one "low" class. The pupils in the heterogeneously grouped classes received their class assignments by being randomly placed in one of four or five first grade classes in the building designated by the regular school district boundaries. Kindergarten teacher predictions of pupil performance were also available on this group. A total of approximately four hundred seventy-five children were involved in the study with one hundred fifteen pupils assigned to the homogeneous classes. The criteria measures selected for evaluation were reading achievement, arithmetic achievement and attitudes toward learning. Information regarding chronological age, readiness test scores, intelligence test results and teacher judgment comprised available independent variable data. In addition, measures of teacher attitudes, the social structure of the class group and the emotional climate of the classroom were gathered as potential covariates. Major findings of the study were  1) F ratios obtained from the analysis of variance indicate a significant difference in favor of homogeneous grouping in the high ability group. This portion of the analysis did not take cognizance of the covariates. 2) Emotional climate of the classroom and the social structure of the class group were found to provide significant covariate data. 3) Inclusion of the covariate data in the multivariate analysis continued to support the value of homogeneous grouping, though the analysis points up the significance of this difference as being in the middle and low ability groups when the covariate effects are taken into account.

references.title_full: Middle School Ability Grouping and Student Achievement in Science and Mathematics
references.authors: Hoffer Thomas B;
references.publisher: SAGE PublicationsSage CA: Los Angeles, CA
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This paper analyzes the effects of middle school ability grouping on cognitive achievement in mathematics and science. In contrast to most previous research on tracking, this analysis compares outcomes in grouped and non-grouped schools. The hypotheses tested here are, first, that ability grouping raises the aggregate level of student achievement and, second, that ability grouping achieves this end by increasing the learning of all students. Comparing average student achievement growth from the seventh to the ninth grades in grouped and non-grouped schools shows that overall gains from ability grouping in either subject are negligible, controlling for differences in student social background and initial levels of achievement. Comparing the achievement growth of non-grouped students and high- and low-group students shows that high-group placement generally has a weak positive effect while low-group placement has a stronger negative effect. Ability grouping thus appears to benefit advanced students, to harm slower students, and to have a negligible overall effect as the benefits and liabilities cancel each other.

references.title_full: Team Teaching and Flexible Grouping in the Junior High-School Social Studies
references.authors: Zweibelson I ; Bahnmuller M ; Lyman L ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Many schools are moving rapidly to make the changes which the schools of tomorrow will require. One of these changes is from the fixed and rigidly involved role of a teacher with a group of students to planned team teaching. Because the junior high school period is one which calls for initial exploration in the understanding and skills leading to effective behavior in a free society, team teaching and flexible grouping seem to be particularly effective methods to use in social studies.

references.title_full: A Comparison of Pupil Achievement in Graded and Nongraded Primary Classrooms
references.authors: Halliwell Joseph W;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The past decade will stand out for educators as a period of marked ferment in education. Although most of the ferment has taken place at the secondary school level, the elementary schools have also been affected greatly. While several noteworthy experimental programs featuring the teaching of foreign languages, the utilizing of an individualized reading program and the adopting of new approaches to the teaching of mathematics in the elementary schools have been undertaken. It was the purpose of this study to determine whether there would be a significant gain in the achievement of primary grade pupils after a variation of the nongraded primary unit was adopted. More specifically, the investigation sought to compare the achievement of 146 primary pupils who had been taught for approximately one year under a nongraded program in reading and spelling with the achievement of 149 primary pupils who had been taught solely within the framework of the graded class structure.

references.title_full: Effects of Administrator Implemented Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Grouping on Reading Achievement of Selected Sixth-Grade Students
references.authors: Thacker Jerry ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Problem. A Nation at Risk reported that the average achievement score of high-school students on most standardized tests is lower now than it was a quarter of a century ago, and the majority of the brightest students fail to achieve according to their ability. A salient problem in educating pupils is that of attaining reading comprehension achievement scores comparable to their intellectual potential. This study examines the effects of administrator implemented homogeneous and heterogeneous grouping on the reading achievement of selected sixth-grade students. Method. This was a quasi-experimental study using parametric techniques. The tests for hypotheses were analysis of variance, analysis of covariance, and multiple linear regression. This study compares the reading comprehension achievement of an experimental group and a control group. It also compares the interaction of gender as a factor in reading achievement due to instructional grouping techniques. There were 113 sixth-grade students in the experimental group and 59 students in the control group. Results. Nine hypotheses were tested for three reading group levels  (1) high ability, (2) average ability, and (3) low ability. Reading achievement was not affected to a statistically significant degree at alpha = .05 by either instructional approach--homogeneous or heterogeneous--regardless of reading group ability level. Hypotheses applicable to both high-ability and average-ability students exposed to homogeneous instruction found no significant differences related to gender. However, low-ability female students scored significantly higher than low-ability male students. Hypotheses applicable to both high-ability and low-ability students exposed to heterogeneous instruction found no significant differences related to gender. However, average-ability male students scored significantly better than average-ability female students. Conclusions. Academic performance, as measured by sixth-grade reading scores, was not affected to a statistically significant degree by the instructional approach--homogeneous or heterogeneous--regardless of reading group ability level. Although there was a degree of inconsistency in regard to gender, average-ability male students tended to perform better in reading classes when exposed to heterogeneous instruction and low-ability female students tended to perform better in reading classes when exposed to homogeneous instruction.

references.title_full: The effects of streaming in the primary school: Comparison of streamed and unstreamed schools
references.authors: Daniels J C;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This investigation seems to indicate that when junior schools adopt a policy of non‐streaming, the result is, on the average, an improvement in the intellectual and scholastic progress of pupils. This increase in ability and attainment is achieved without any noticeable ‘holding back’ of brighter pupils, though it seems true that the main effect of non‐streaming is a radical ‘pulling up’ of the more backward children. These results are in striking contrast with what teachers believe to be the effects of streaming, as shown in Part I of this article. Streaming, most junior school teachers believe, is a method of school organisation which allows children to progress, educationally, ‘at their own natural pace’  bright children are, it is believed, held back by being taught in classes containing duller pupils, whilst duller pupils tend to be overawed, and consequently are retarded, by the presence of brighter pupils in their classes. Consequently, it is widely believed that both dull, average and bright pupils make maximum educational progress when streaming policies are operated. The evidence of this investigation suggests that streaming does not in fact have these effects—rather that the contrary is true. In view of the fact that streaming procedures at the junior stage of education do not find favour in most other advanced countries of the world whilst they are almost universally practised in English junior schools, it would seem that further research into the effects of streaming along the lines of the present investigation, are urgently needed.

references.abstract: This investigation seems to indicate that when junior schools adopt a policy of non‐streaming, the result is, on the average, an improvement in the intellectual and scholastic progress of pupils. This increase in ability and attainment is achieved without any noticeable ‘holding back’ of brighter pupils, though it seems true that the main effect of non‐streaming is a radical ‘pulling up’ of the more backward children. These results are in striking contrast with what teachers believe to be the effects of streaming, as shown in Part I of this article. Streaming, most junior school teachers believe, is a method of school organisation which allows children to progress, educationally, ‘at their own natural pace’  bright children are, it is believed, held back by being taught in classes containing duller pupils, whilst duller pupils tend to be overawed, and consequently are retarded, by the presence of brighter pupils in their classes. Consequently, it is widely believed that both dull, average and bright pupils make maximum educational progress when streaming policies are operated. The evidence of this investigation suggests that streaming does not in fact have these effects—rather that the contrary is true. In view of the fact that streaming procedures at the junior stage of education do not find favour in most other advanced countries of the world whilst they are almost universally practised in English junior schools, it would seem that further research into the effects of streaming along the lines of the present investigation, are urgently needed.

references.title_full: Ability Grouping And Its Effect Upon Individual Achievement
references.authors: Loomer Bradley Max A X;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate one specific type of homogeneous grouping. The grouping procedure employed in this investigation centered around careful consideration of such factors as intelligence quotient, mental age, chronological age, reading achievement level, composite rating of a standardized basic skills test, teacher appraisal of ability, sex, and the school administrator's judgment. Each pupil in grades four, five, and six was categorized as belonging to one of five ability levels designated bright, above average, average, below average, and low by the principals, teachers, and the writer. In schools where there was more than one section per grade these levels were used as the basis for sectioning. In one class section were placed all pupils, of a specific grade, who were identified as belonging to the bright ability level. In another section, separate from the one containing the bright pupils, the pupils identified as belonging to the low ability class were placed. Grouped along with the bright ability level pupils were other students of the same grade who were identified as belonging to the ability levels designated as above average, average, and below average.  The results of this analysis verified that all heterogeneous classes encompassed pupils from all five ability levels. For each pupil in the study the following information was collected  a) IQ  b) Grade  c ) Age  d) Mental Age  f ) Iowa Tests of Basic Skills for all areas of the test ( i.e. Vocabulary, Reading, Language, Work Study, Arithmetic , and Composite.) This study devoted itself to the overall group comparisons between those students in the homogeneous and heterogeneous classes who were identified as belonging to the same ability levels. To test the significance between all group comparisons the F statistic using analysis of variance procedures was employed. The results, in general, do not lend support to the claimed advantage of grouping as opposed to no grouping. The evidence presented seems to indicate that pupils, for the most part, are not affected by the administrative procedure commonly described as homogeneous grouping. The fact that the homogeneous classes did not achieve significantly more than did the heterogeneous classes does not automatically rule out any advantages to the grouping procedure. It may well be that the instructional task was made easier by having the extremely bright in one room and the extremely low in another room. The evidence presented in this study indicates no decided advantage of this method of grouping over a random method of assigning pupils to classes. The evidence seems to indicate that grouping is merely an administrative device employed to serve the schools in assigning pupils to classes. If there are advantages accruing to this procedure, they must be found in areas other than those measurable by a standardized test of basic skills. The key to good education of children evidently rests with good teaching. This study points this out by showing that the grouping procedure does not by and in itself produce greater gains by students, at least those in grades four, five, and six.

references.title_full: An Experiment on Homogeneous Grouping for Reading in Elementary Classes
references.authors: Berkun Mitchell M; Swanson Lloyd W; Sawyer David M;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: About 1100 children in the third, fourth, and fifth grades were tested for reading achievement level in April after half of them spent the school year in experimentally homogeneous classes and the other half in control classes containing a full range of reading ability. Pupils in the experimentally homogeneous classes achieved an average of 0.4 year higher reading level than did the control classes, a statistically significant effect. There was a tendency for this advantage of grouping to be larger in the fifth grade and to be larger among those initially above average in reading level, but even the initially-below-average children demonstrated a significant advantage of the homogeneous grouping. Classification discrepancies between alternate forms of the California Reading Test were almost non-existent.

references.title_full: Effects of Administrator Implemented Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Grouping on Reading Achievement of Selected Sixth-Grade Students
references.authors: Thacker Jerry ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Problem. A Nation at Risk reported that the average achievement score of high-school students on most standardized tests is lower now than it was a quarter of a century ago, and the majority of the brightest students fail to achieve according to their ability. A salient problem in educating pupils is that of attaining reading comprehension achievement scores comparable to their intellectual potential. This study examines the effects of administrator implemented homogeneous and heterogeneous grouping on the reading achievement of selected sixth-grade students. Method. This was a quasi-experimental study using parametric techniques. The tests for hypotheses were analysis of variance, analysis of covariance, and multiple linear regression. This study compares the reading comprehension achievement of an experimental group and a control group. It also compares the interaction of gender as a factor in reading achievement due to instructional grouping techniques. There were 113 sixth-grade students in the experimental group and 59 students in the control group. Results. Nine hypotheses were tested for three reading group levels  (1) high ability, (2) average ability, and (3) low ability. Reading achievement was not affected to a statistically significant degree at alpha = .05 by either instructional approach--homogeneous or heterogeneous--regardless of reading group ability level. Hypotheses applicable to both high-ability and average-ability students exposed to homogeneous instruction found no significant differences related to gender. However, low-ability female students scored significantly higher than low-ability male students. Hypotheses applicable to both high-ability and low-ability students exposed to heterogeneous instruction found no significant differences related to gender. However, average-ability male students scored significantly better than average-ability female students. Conclusions. Academic performance, as measured by sixth-grade reading scores, was not affected to a statistically significant degree by the instructional approach--homogeneous or heterogeneous--regardless of reading group ability level. Although there was a degree of inconsistency in regard to gender, average-ability male students tended to perform better in reading classes when exposed to heterogeneous instruction and low-ability female students tended to perform better in reading classes when exposed to homogeneous instruction.

references.title_full: The Educational Achievement of Pupils in Differentiated and Undifferentiated Groups
references.authors: Breidenstine A G;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: In brief, the study seeks to present evidence concerning the educational achievement of both the differentiated and the undifferentiated groups in grades two to nine inclusive. Eleven schools participated in this investigation, four practicing differentiation and seven undifferentiation. These schools provided 2,325 children from grades two to nine inclusive. In undifferentiated classes there were 1,163 pupils and 1,162 in differentiated classes. The number of pupils was reduced to 787 for each group by matching for grade and intelligence. The eleven schools furnished the intelligence quotients. The New Stanford Achievement Tests were used to measure the educational achievement. The test data and the intelligence quotients were the sources from which were determined the accomplishment ratio, the educational quotient, the composite score, and the correlation between the intelligence quotients and the educational quotients. The results were tabulated and described for each grade of each group and for the total.

references.title_full: A Study of Achievement as a Function of Homogeneous Grouping
references.authors: Koontz William F;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Early attempts at class grouping were executed with no empirical proof of its efficacy  and even today, there is inconclusive evidence as to the instructional value of homogeneous grouping. Approximately 25 years ago, it was reported that the literature related to homogeneous grouping had been carefully reviewed, and the most significant conclusion from it all was how little it had brought of clearly incontestable knowledge"(3). Professor Passow, in 1956, stated that there was no" significant unanimity of findings" in this area. The purpose of this study w as to test the null hypothesis that children grouped homogeneously by subject matter achievement, and who were given instructional materials on their achievement level, would show no greater achievement as a result than pupils who were grouped heterogeneously. On the basis of the evidence gathered in this study, this hypothesis cannot be rejected. Here, too, as in many other studies, homogeneous grouping failed to realize its theoretical possibilities. Experimental and control pupils were closely matched in terms of achievement at the beginning of the experiment. However, it may be that many variables that need to be controlled in experimentation with human behavior evaded control in this study.

references.title_full: Three Approaches to Grouping Procedures for the Education of Disadvantaged Primary School Children
references.authors: Cartwright G Phillip; McIntosh Dean K;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purpose of the study was to investigate the relative effects of three different grouping procedures (heterogeneous, homogeneous, and flexible) on the academic achievement of disadvantaged primary school children. All 260 pupils were randomly assigned to one of three treatment groups taught by nine teachers. The conclusion from the 2-year study was that there were no differences in academic achievement attributable to the three different grouping patterns employed.

references.title_full: Ability Grouping Effects on Academic Achievement and Self-Esteem in a Southwestern School District
references.authors: Abadzi Helen ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The effects of ability grouping on the academic achievement and self-esteem of fourth-grade students were assessed through regression-discontinuity analysis in a Texas school district which used a cutoff score for placement in high and regular ability groups. Standardized achievement test scores of high ability students showed a significant increase after a year of ability grouping. Students who had scored a little above the criterion showed performance increase, while students who had scored a little below the criterion showed a decrease after a year in regular ability classes. The self-esteem was assessed near the beginning and end of the fourth grade. No significant differences were found from the beginning to the end of the fourth grade or between the high and regular groups after third grade achievement test scores were covaried.

references.title_full: A comparative study of mentally gifted children heterogeneously and homogeneously grouped
references.authors: Bell ME ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This investigation sought to discover the differences in growth, if any, of 30 mentally gifted children in a homogeneous group as compared with 30 mentally gifted children heterogeneously grouped. In an attempt to measure the differences of growth of the children in the two groups, these specific questions were considered  1. What differences can be discovered in certain basic personality traits of self-adjustment between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? 2. What differences can be discovered in certain basic personality traits of social adjustment between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? 3. What differences can be discovered in the types and degrees of mental health liabilities between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? 4. What differences can be discovered in the types and degrees of mental health assets between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? 5. What differences can be discovered in the work 6. What differences can be discovered in achievement in reading, vocabulary, arithmetic fundamentals , arithmetic problem solving, English, and spelling between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? The subjects in this investigation comprised two groups. One was the homogeneous group composed of those children in a homogeneous group for mentally gifted children in grade five. These subjects had recorded I.Q. measures of 125 or higher on the Henmon-Nelson Test of Mental Ability and the Stanford-Binet Individual Test, were in good health, and had their parents1 consent to be in this group. The other group was the control group, the subjects being in classrooms with heterogeneous groups. This group was selected on the basis of I.Q. measures comparable to those of the children in the homogeneous group (within a range of 10 points) as determined by the results on the Kenmon-Ne1son Test of Mental Ability and the Stanford-Binet Individual Test. The study skills between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? subjects in this group also matched the subjects in the homogeneous group through similar grade placement, same or similar age, and comparable geographical locations, and they also had parental consent to participate in the study. This research utilised the techniques of between group comparison based on the result of test scores. Data were secured by using a work sheet to record identification data and scheduling data, such as name of child, name of school, name of test, and time and date of testing. Two testings were given to each group for comparison purposes. The following series of tests were used  California Test of Personality, Revision Mental Health Analysis, Iowa Every-Pupil Tests of Basic Skills, Work-Study Skills, Metropolitan Achievement Tests, In this way the comparison should more nearly represent the highest degree of validity. From the data examined and the achievements shown in the tests, the following conclusions are given concerning the six specific questions. 1. What differences can be discovered in certain basic personality traits of self adjustment between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? At the beginning of the experimental period, the first test showed there was no significant difference between the means of the two groups. The individual components of the self-adjustment for the homogeneous group changed and improved, while those for the heterogeneous group remained practically the same. The greatest change in the homogeneous group occurred in the area of freedom from nervous tendencies, while in the other group there was slight improvement. Generally, it can be concluded that homogeneity has no real effect upon the personality traits of self-adjustment. 2. What differences can be discovered in certain basic personality traits of social adjustment between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? There was no significant difference between the groups at the beginning or at the end of the experimental period. The personality tests indicate there was no significant difference between the homogeneous and heterogeneous groups either before or after the experimental period. According to the results of the California Test of Personality, no statistically significant difference existed between the means of the raw scores of the two groups. What differences can be discovered in the types and degrees of mental health liabilities between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? When tested by the Liabilities Section of the Mental Health Analysis Test the homogeneous and the heterogeneous groups showed no statistically significant difference between the means.  4. What differences can be discovered in the types and degrees of mental health assets between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? The results of the Mental Health Analysis Test seem to show that the gifted child’s mental health is far above that of the average child. 5. What differences can be discovered in the work-study skills between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? In determining the differences in achievement in work study skills of the experimental and control groups, the Iowa Test of Basle Skills (Test B) was given. Map reading, use of references, use of the index, use of the dictionary, and reading graphs, charts, and tables were the skills tested. The tests indicated little difference between the groups and the national norms.  6. What differences can be discovered in achievement in reading, vocabulary, arithmetic fundamentals, arithmetic problem solving. English, and spelling between the heterogeneous and homogeneous groups? The Metropolitan Achievement tests were used for determining achievement in reading, vocabulary, arithmetic fundamentals, arithmetic problem solving, English, and spelling.  The significant difference at the end of the testing period between the means of the total average grade equivalents leads one to conclude that the homogeneous group in this study tended to achieve a slightly higher grade equivalent level than did the heterogeneous group. In reading, the difference between the means of each group was significant at the fourth grade level, in favor of the heterogeneous group. The vocabulary test showed no significant difference between the two groups either when the tests were first given or at the close of the period. In arithmetic fundamentals, the first testing revealed no significant difference between the two groups, but the final testing showed that the experimental group exceeded the control group significantly. The results of the English tests followed closely the results of the vocabulary tests. The mean differences between the groups at the beginning and at the end of the test period were significant. Even though the t-ratios may seem to have increased, no conclusion to the effect of homogeneity can be drawn because a statistically distinct change is not revealed. In the light of the discrepancies of the correlation of I.Q.’s with the achievement test results the tendency to conclude that homogeneity has influenced the English test scores of the mentally gifted child cannot be fully supported. However, the second test showed the difference between the means of the two groups to be significant in favor of the homogeneous group. After examining the data and the results of this study the conclusion that homogeneity has a pronounced effect upon the achievement of the mentally gifted child cannot be fully supported. Significant mean differences between the homogeneous and heterogeneous groups are present, but since not all subtests of the achievement test results exhibit this significance, the positive effect of homogeneity is weakened.

references.title_full: A Comparison of Pupil Achievement in Graded and Nongraded Primary Classrooms
references.authors: Halliwell Joseph W;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The past decade will stand out for educators as a period of marked ferment in education. Although most of the ferment has taken place at the secondary school level, the elementary schools have also been affected greatly. While several noteworthy experimental programs featuring the teaching of foreign languages, the utilizing of an individualized reading program and the adopting of new approaches to the teaching of mathematics in the elementary schools have been undertaken. It was the purpose of this study to determine whether there would be a significant gain in the achievement of primary grade pupils after a variation of the nongraded primary unit was adopted. More specifically, the investigation sought to compare the achievement of 146 primary pupils who had been taught for approximately one year under a nongraded program in reading and spelling with the achievement of 149 primary pupils who had been taught solely within the framework of the graded class structure.

references.title_full: Intraclass grouping for reading instruction: Who Makes the Decisions and Why?
references.authors: Nichols N ;
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The focus of this project was to compare the effectiveness of three methods of teaching reading to primary pupils. The data to be discussed were part of the data collected at the end of the second year of the study. The following unique situation occurred withing one of the three treatment groups. One of the cooperating schools had been using a plan of interclass grouping for reading instruction at first and second grade levels before the project began and continued the practice throughout the study. That is, pupils were randomly assigned to one of three homeroom classes. For reading instruction they were reassigned to one of the three teachers on the basis of readiness and of intelligence test scores. The superior pupils were assigned to one teacher, the average to another, and the below average to the third. The superior and below average groups participated in the Cooperative Research Project. At two other schools that were taking part in the project there were two other classrooms of children that almost exactly matched these two classes in terms of readiness and of intelligence measures. The pupils in these rooms had been randomly assigned to their class from the pool making up the several classes at that grade level. The achievement differences are overwhelmingly in favor of those pupils who were randomly assigned and received instruction in their own self-contained classroom. Their achievement actually equals that of the class identified as superior in the school with interclass ability grouping. The probability of the differences that are shown being due to measurement error is extremely small. Interclass grouping, with its alleged reduced range of variability and hence instructional needs, did not show any benefit for these below average pupils after two years of primary instruction.

references.title_full: Promoting foundation reading skills with at-risk students
references.authors: Sucena Ana  Silva Ana Filipa  Marques Cátia
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This paper presents an early reading intervention program, the PPCL ( Programa de Promoção das Competências Leitoras —Promoting Reading Skills Program). PPCL focuses on the promotion of reading foundation abilities—letter-sound, phonemic awareness, decoding, and spelling—with at-risk first graders. This study assessed the impact of PPCL on the reading foundation abilities with 311 first graders (173 boys and 138 girls), divided between intervention and comparative group (respectively, 206 and 105 first graders). Results were analyzed with an inter- (intervention and comparative group) and intra- (pre-and post-test) group design. A mixed two-way Manova indicated the presence of statistically significant differences between the two assessment moments, with the intervention group presenting higher values than the comparative group in all abilities at the post-test and also above the cutoff score in all variables, which indicates that at-risk students eventually concluded the school year with satisfactory levels of reading skills. On the other hand, the comparative group scored below the cutoff score in all variables. The magnitude of the effect on the intervention group was higher than the one observed in the comparative group. Reading promotion with PPCL significantly improved at-risk students reading skills. In future studies, the authors intend to follow up on reading and writing participants’ skills.

references.title_full: Effects of a supplemental intervention focused in equivalency concepts for students with varying abilities
references.authors: Hunt Jessica H
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a Tier 2 supplemental intervention focused on rational number equivalency concepts and applications on the mathematics performance of third-grade students with and without mathematics difficulties. The researcher used a pretest–posttest control group design and random assignment of 19 participants to core instruction and 19 participants to core + intervention instruction. Intervention instruction included the ratio interpretation of rational number in conjunction with explicit and conceptual instructional components—judicious review opportunities, concrete and visual representations, systematic task progression focused on big ideas, teacher and student verbalizations, and multiple opportunities for practice—to deliver a sequence of 20 intervention sessions over a period of 4 weeks. Students receiving core instruction plus intervention outperformed those receiving only core instruction on a standard measure of the intervention content as well as a pretest–posttest measure reflective of the core curriculum.

references.title_full: Enhancing the vocabulary knowledge of first-grade children with supplemental booster instruction
references.authors: Puhalla Eve M
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This study examined the effects of instructional intensity on the acquisition of storybook vocabulary in first graders who were at risk of early reading failure. It also measured whether the intervention was effective for closing the vocabulary knowledge gap between students who were at risk and their average-achieving peers. A total of 66 students participated in the study, 44 identified as at risk and 22 as average-achieving peers. Students identified as at risk were randomly assigned to either a booster group, where they received explicit instruction of selected storybook vocabulary, or a no booster group, where they received vocabulary instruction in the context of read alouds through an experimental Read Aloud curriculum. A repeated measures design was employed to compare the effects of the intervention. Results indicate that students in the booster group significantly outperformed the students in the no booster and average-achieving peers groups on storybook vocabulary measures.

references.title_full: Remedial early numeracy education  can children identified as having a language deficiency benefit?
references.title_parent: International Journal Of Language & Communication Disorders
references.authors: Van Luit Johannes E. H  Toll Sylke W.M
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: Abstract Background Growing attention has been paid to the possibility of supporting early numeracy in at‐risk kindergartners. Furthermore, it is assumed that language proficiency is an important prerequisite in early maths skills. Aims To examine whether remedial early numeracy education in kindergarten, which has been proven to be effective in general, is also beneficial for children with a language deficiency. Methods &amp  Procedures Based on intensive selection, four different conditions were included  two groups received remedial education, one consisting of children being language proficient ( N = 86) and one of children with a language deficiency ( N = 26), and two groups followed the regular curriculum, one consisting of children being language proficient ( N = 51) and one of children with a language deficiency ( N = 24). Remedial education was for 1.5 school years (90 sessions, 30 min per session, twice per week), following the programme ‘The Road to Mathematics’. During this period, the children receiving remedial education did not attend the regular maths lessons in the classroom, which were offered for at least 1 h per week. Effects were assessed for early numeracy and mathematical skills (operationalized as basic calculation fluency) in kindergarten and first grade. Outcomes &amp  Results Three analyses of covariance (ANCOVAs) revealed that, when accounting for achievement at pre‐test, children with a language deficiency who received remedial numeracy education performed better on early numeracy skills in kindergarten and first grade than kindergartners with a language deficiency that followed the regular curriculum. Furthermore, they were able to catch up with their language proficient peers in early numeracy. However, children with a language deficiency who received remedial numeracy education did not differ from children who followed the regular curriculum on mathematical skills, suggesting that benefits for numeracy did not generalize to more advanced skills of addition and subtraction. Conclusions &amp  Implications Since, in general, it can be concluded that early numeracy education is indeed effective for kindergartners with a language deficiency, this study finds evidence that intensive support is desirable for children with delayed or impaired language development.

references.title_full: Assessing the efficacy of a Tier 2 early intervention for transcription skills in Spanish elementary school students
references.authors: Jiménez Juan E  de León Sara C  García Eduardo  Seoane Rocío C
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The main objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of a Tier 2 intervention within the context of the Response to Intervention (RtI) model implemented by Spanish first- to second-grade primary school teachers to improve at-risk students’ transcription skills. Teachers were instructed in the administration of a writing curriculum-based measure composed of 5 isolates measures (allographs, dictated words with arbitrary spelling or non-ruled, dictated words with rule-based spelling, dictated nonsense words, and dictated sentences) to identify at-risk students and to monitor their progress  and in the implementation of a systematic and explicit instructional program to improve transcription skills in at-risk students. A total of 164 at-risk students from 12 schools from the Canary Islands participated in the study. Teachers were provided with a support system that included a web-based training program for writing. Implementation fidelity was analyzed using direct observations and self-reports. All students were assessed three times during the academic year. In a hierarchical linear growth modeling procedure, differences in growth rates of transcription skills were compared between students who received the intervention, those who did not, and their typically achieving peers. Additionally, the effects of the intervention in the experimental at-risk group were also analyzed, differentiating between those who left the risk status and those who remained at-risk. Children at-risk in the intervention condition appeared to benefit more in handwriting skills than at-risk children in the control condition, but to a lesser extent in spelling accuracy. Nevertheless, improvements in both transcription skills had only been made in the experimental risk group that had left the risk situation.

references.title_full: A kindergarten number-sense intervention with contrasting practice conditions for low-achieving children
references.title_parent: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education
references.authors: Dyson Nancy  Jordan Nancy C  Beliakoff Amber  Hassinger‐Das Brenna
references.publisher: National Council of Teachers of Mathematics
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The efficacy of a research-based number-sense intervention for low-achieving kinder-gartners was examined. Children (N = 126) were randomly assigned to 1 of 3 conditions  a number-sense intervention followed by a number-fact practice session, an identical number-sense intervention followed by a number-list practice session, or a business-as-usual control group. The interventions were delivered in a small-group setting over 24 half-hour lessons. Both intervention groups performed better than controls on measures of number sense, arithmetic fluency, and general mathematics calculation achievement at immediate posttest. However, the number-fact practice condition gave children an additional advantage over the number-list practice condition on the outcomes at delayed posttest 8 weeks later. The number-fact practice condition was especially effective for producing gains in English learners.

references.title_full: Effects of remedial numeracy instruction throughout kindergarten starting at different ages  Evidence from a large-scale longitudinal study
references.authors: Toll Sylke W.M  Van Luit Johannes E. H
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The aims of this study are to investigate the effects of remedial numeracy support throughout kindergarten, and to compare the effects of interventions from different lengths. Support occurred two times per week for either 1.5 (90 sessions  complete condition) or 0.5 school years (28 sessions  short condition). Below-average students were randomly assigned to complete intervention (N = 155), short intervention (N = 105), or control (systematically offered education-as-usual  N = 150). Accounting for achievements at pretest, children who received one of the interventions outperformed the control children in early numeracy at post-test and follow-up, suggesting that children internalized the learned knowledge. Transfer effects on simple arithmetic were only found in the complete support group, whereas both interventions were effective for complex mathematics.

references.title_full: Improving at-risk learners' understanding of fractions
references.authors: Fuchs Lynn S  Schumacher Robin F  Long Jessica  Namkung Jessica  Hamlett Carol L  Cirino Paul T  Jordan Nancy C  Siegler Robert  Gersten Russell  Changas Paul
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: The purposes of this study were to investigate the effects of an intervention designed to improve at-risk 4th graders’ understanding of fractions and to examine the processes by which effects occurred. The intervention focused more on the measurement interpretation of fractions  the control condition focused more on the part-whole interpretation of fractions and on procedures. Intervention was also designed to compensate for at-risk students’ limitations in the domain-general abilities associated with fraction learning. At-risk students (n ⫽ 259) were randomly assigned to intervention and control. Whole-number calculation skill, domain-general abilities (working memory, attentive behavior, processing speed, listening comprehension), and fraction proficiency were pretested. Intervention occurred for 12 weeks, 3 times per week, 30 min per session, and then fraction performance was reassessed. On each conceptual and procedural fraction outcome, effects favored intervention over control (effect sizes ⫽ 0.29 to 2.50), and the gap between at-risk and low-risk students narrowed for the intervention group but not the control group. Improvement in the accuracy of children’s measurement interpretation of fractions mediated intervention effects. Also, intervention effects were moderated by domain-general abilities, but not whole-number calculation skill.

references.title_full: Effects of small group tutoring with and without validated classroom instruction on at-risk students' math problem solving  are two tiers of prevention better than one?
references.authors: Fuchs Lynn S  Fuchs Douglas  Craddock Caitlin  Hollenbeck Kurstin N  Hamlett Carol L  Schatschneider Christopher
references.subject: toolkit
references.abstract: This study assessed the effects of small-group tutoring with and without validated classroom instruction on at-risk students' math problem solving. Stratifying within schools, 119 3rd-grade classes were randomly assigned to conventional or validated problem-solving instruction (Hot Math, schema-broadening instruction). Students identified as at risk (n = 243) were randomly assigned, within classroom conditions, to receive or not receive Hot Math tutoring. Students were tested on problem-solving and math applications measures before and after 16 weeks of intervention. Analyses of variance, which accounted for the nested structure of the data, revealed that the tutored students who received validated classroom instruction achieved better than the tutored students who received conventional classroom instruction (effect size = 1.34). However, the advantage for tutoring over no tutoring was similar whether students received validated or conventional classroom instruction (effect sizes = 1.18 and 1.13). Tutoring, not validated classroom instruction, reduced the prevalence of math difficulty. Implications for responsiveness-to-intervention prevention models and for enhancing math problem-solving instruction are discussed.

references.title_full: The effects of rime- and phoneme-based teaching delivered by Learning Support Assistants
